claim: MTD changes a network's addresses, layout and software.
quote: Many MTD techniques, including Internet Protocol (IP) mutation, network topology changes, platform migration, and software stack shufﬂing, change the attack surface

claim: MTD changes credentials, so that stolen credentials go out of date.
quote: The example system or network attributes that can be changed include instruction sets [95], [132], address space layouts [144], IP addresses [3], [12], [87], [97], [147], port numbers [107], proxies [91], virtual machines [22], [177], operating systems [157], or software programs [84].
issue: Cho never names credentials as a moving element: not in the 'what to move' list, not in Table III, not in the SDR definitions (credentials appear only as something redundancy+diversity makes the attacker need more of). Nearest is the 'revocability' metric (expiring a prior configuration, e.g. access control), which is a metric, not a claim that MTD rotates credentials.
fix_text: "addresses, layout, software and credentials" -> "addresses, layout and software"; "so that stolen credentials and reconnaissance go out of date" -> "so that reconnaissance goes out of date" (or add-source for credential rotation)

claim: MTD makes reconnaissance go out of date.
quote: by making information collected by the attackers obsolete or by wasting attackers resources in the collection of useless information
issue: Said of shuffling-based MTD; reconnaissance is the information collected.

claim: MTD moves on a schedule, so it works even if the attacker is never detected.
quote: The proactive adaptation triggers MTD techniques by changing conﬁgurations or properties on a schedule ... Proactive MTD moves regardless of the presence of an attacker
locator: Sec. II-B, p. 713 printed (PDF p. 5); p. 714 printed (PDF p. 6)
issue: True of Cho's proactive MTD only; Cho's MTD also includes reactive MTD, which assumes the attacker is detected. Acceptable for a thesis about scheduled MTD, but the sentence states it of MTD in general.

claim: Most MTD tests run in simulation.
quote: Most studies evaluating the performance of MTD approaches have been validated based on simulation experiments.
issue: Corpus is Cho's 2011-2018 works; present tense rests on the co-cited jalowski2026.

claim: Those tests use attacker models far simpler than an APT.
quote: Generally, it is assumed that attackers have certain attack patterns, rather than that they learn and can launch adaptive attacks. ... Most attack behaviors considered in the existing MTD works occur during the reconnaissance stage.
locator: Sec. V-D; Sec. X, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15); p. 738 printed (PDF p. 30)
issue: Cho lists limitations (fixed attack patterns, no learning, few multi-strategy scenarios, reconnaissance-stage attacks) but never compares the attacker models to an APT, and Sec. V-A says the opposite in part: 'In the existing MTD works, we found that attackers are persistent ... (e.g., APT attacks' and APT 'has been commonly considered'. 'Far simpler than an APT' is the dissertation's synthesis; Cho also does not tie the simple models to simulation specifically.
fix_text: "against attacker models far simpler than an APT" -> "against attacker models that follow fixed attack patterns" (or let jalowski2026 carry the APT comparison, if it does)

claim: MTD is the timely change of the system configurations an attacker relies on.
quote: this goal is achieved via MTD by the manipulation of multiple system conﬁgurations to modify and control the attack surface, where the attacker engages with the system ... ‘When to move’ involves deciding the optimal time to change from the current state of an MTD system to a new state, invalidating information or progress gained by an attacker in the current state.
locator: Sec. I-A; Sec. II-B, p. 709 printed (PDF p. 1); p. 713 printed (PDF p. 5)
issue: 'Timely' is carried by Cho's 'when to move' (optimal time), not by its definition sentence; 'relies on' paraphrases 'engages with'.

claim: An MTD is designed by answering three questions: what to move, how to move and when to move.
quote: The fundamental design principle for developing MTD techniques lies in the decisions for the following three key questions [24]: what to move , how to move , and when to move .
issue: Cho attributes the three questions to its [24]: Cai, Wang, Hu and Wang, 'Moving target defense: State of the art and characteristics', Front. Inf. Technol. Electron. Eng. 17(11), 2016. NB this is NOT the bib's cai2016 (Cai, Wang, Luo and Hu, GSPN model, Advanced Computer Architecture 2016); do not 'cite-primary' with that key.

claim: Redundancy replicates components, so that service survives a compromise.
quote: This technique provides multiple replicas of system (or network) components ... by providing redundant ways of providing the same services when some of the network nodes or system components are compromised
issue: Cho credits the SDR labels to Hong and Kim [76] (hongkim2016, cited in U0054); the definition is Cho's own wording.

claim: A proactive MTD moves on a schedule; a reactive MTD moves in response to an event such as an intrusion alert; a hybrid MTD adapts its schedule to such events while bounding the time between moves.
quote: The reactive adaptation is based on an event or an alert that executes the adaptation as a response to a message from the detection of suspicious activity. ... The proactive adaptation triggers MTD techniques by changing conﬁgurations or properties on a schedule, with either ﬁxed or random intervals between adaptations. ... the time interval to trigger an MTD operation is adaptive upon certain events or security alerts while the interval is also bounded in length to prevent potential, undetected security threats [184]
locator: Sec. II-B, p. 713 printed (PDF p. 5); p. 714 printed (PDF p. 6)
issue: Hybrid definition carries Cho's [184], but is stated in Cho's own definitional voice.

claim: Deploying MTD too often costs service availability.
quote: triggering MTD operations too often naturally leads to reducing service availability and interrupting seamless service provision

claim: Deploying MTD too rarely gives the attacker time.
quote: If the interval time is too long, then an attacker may be allowed a sufﬁcient amount of time to scan a system and then penetrate into the system, resulting in a security breach.
issue: Cho's hedge 'may be allowed' is softened to a flat 'gives'; does not change the point.

claim: An MTD evaluation has three parts that use the attacker model (modelling approaches, metrics, evaluation methods), as surveyed by Cho.
quote: In this work, we discuss key modeling and solution techniques of MTD based on the following theoretical approaches ... In this section, we discuss what metrics have been used to assess the effectiveness and efﬁciency of the existing MTD techniques. ... In this section, we discuss how the performance of MTD techniques have been assessed based on the following evaluation methods
locator: Secs. VI-VIII, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15); p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19); p. 730 printed (PDF p. 22)
issue: Cho surveys the three topics (Secs. VI, VII, VIII), but never calls them parts of an MTD evaluation, never says each uses the attacker model, and frames Sec. VI as techniques for developing MTD, not evaluating it. The roadmap framing is ours; the cite invites reading it as Cho's.
fix_text: "the three parts of an MTD evaluation that use the attacker model \citep{cho2020}" -> "the three parts of an MTD evaluation that use the attacker model, each a topic Cho et al. survey \citep{cho2020}"

claim: Cho et al. identify three modelling approaches: game theory, genetic algorithms and machine learning, with game theory dominating by volume.
quote: we discuss key modeling and solution techniques of MTD based on the following theoretical approaches: (1) game theory; (2) genetic algorithms; and (3) machine learning. ... A large volume of game theoretic MTD approaches ... game theoretic approaches are dominantly employed in developing MTD
locator: Sec. VI; Sec. VI-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15); p. 726 printed (PDF p. 18); p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19)
issue: Cho calls them the 'key' techniques and notes other MTD works use none of the three (Sec. VI-C end); 'identify three' does not claim exhaustiveness. The 'from-memory' trail is confirmed.

claim: Game theory models the attacker and defender as rational players, each choosing the strategy that maximises its payoff.
quote: Game theory can appropriately model decisions and actions by the defender and attacker, where they are assumed rational and aim to seek optimal strategies to maximize their utilities.

claim: Attackers are not necessarily rational: many aim only to exhaust a system's resources.
quote: attackers may not necessarily be rational or intelligent. Instead, the volume of attackers can be substantially large even if their intelligence is very low, aiming only to waste resources of a system (or network)
issue: Cho's 'the volume of attackers can be substantially large' is a possibility; 'many aim only' asserts it as fact. Hedge dropped.
fix_text: "many aim only to exhaust" -> "many may aim only to exhaust"

claim: A strategy found against a rational attacker may not work against irrational attackers.
quote: if incentives based on rationality are not compatible (e.g., attackers are not stimulated by the incentives), the best strategies derived by the defender may not work for irrational attackers.

claim: Genetic algorithms search over defence configurations for the one with the highest attack resilience and diversity.
quote: Crouse and Fulp [40] employed a GA to identify a secure computer conﬁguration (e.g., OSes or applications) with high diversity in time and space. ... Based on the attack resilience, a top ranked computer conﬁguration is selected. ... GA-based MTD for identifying the optimal deployment of system conﬁgurations
locator: Sec. VI-B; Sec. VI-D, p. 725 printed (PDF p. 17); p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19)
issue: Cho's own general statement is only 'identifying the optimal deployment of system configurations'. The attack-resilience-and-diversity criterion is one primary study's fitness (Crouse and Fulp [40], with Zhuang et al. [185] on diversity), generalised to all GAs. Partly secondary.
fix_text: "for the one with the highest attack resilience and diversity" -> "for the optimal one, scored for example on attack resilience and diversity"

claim: Machine learning learns a deployment strategy from the observed network state.
quote: ML-based MTD to hinder an attacker’s learning or select a best defense strategy ... The high performance of ML in learning attack patterns or identifying optimal solutions is attractive when a large volume of data is available.
locator: Sec. VI-D; Sec. VI-C, p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19)
issue: Cho supports 'ML selects a best defence strategy', learning from data or attack patterns. 'From the observed network state' is not Cho's wording (nearest: Tozer et al. build an MDP 'using the system's components and behaviors'); Cho also gives ML a second role, hindering the attacker's learning, which the sentence drops (deliberately, per the round-24 trail).
fix_text: "from the observed network state" -> "from observed data"

claim: Migrating a service across diverse platforms defends against persistent attacks but can weaken the defence against fast ones.
quote: Carter et al. [26], [27] used game theory to derive an optimal migration strategy. ... although platform diversity is effective against some persistent attacks, it may have a negative impact on the ability to defend against fast and local attacks [26]
issue: Carter, Okhravi and Riordan's finding (Cho [26]: 'Quantitative analysis of active cyber defenses based on temporal platform diversity', arXiv 1401.8255, 2014), reported by Cho; Carter is not in the bib. Two hedges dropped as well: 'some persistent attacks' -> 'persistent attacks', and 'fast and local attacks' -> 'fast ones'.
fix_text: "defends against persistent attacks but can weaken the defence against fast ones" -> "defends against some persistent attacks but can weaken the defence against fast, local ones" (cite-primary would need Carter et al. 2014, a new source)

claim: Cho et al. classify MTD metrics as effectiveness or efficiency metrics, each either attacker-side or defender-side.
quote: we discuss what metrics have been used to assess the effectiveness and efﬁciency of the existing MTD techniques. ... We discuss the metrics to measure the effectiveness of MTD techniques in terms of the perspectives of an attacker and a defender. ... The attacker’s metrics are used to capture how much cost (or penalty) is introduced for an attacker ... The defender’s metrics to measure MTD efﬁciency
locator: Sec. VII; VII-A; VII-B, p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19); p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21)

claim: Attacker-side effectiveness metrics measure the attacker's progress, such as ASP and MTTC.
quote: The attacker’s metric estimates its attack performance ... Attack success probability (ASP) ... Mean time to compromise a system (MTTC)
issue: 'Progress' paraphrases Cho's 'attack performance'; both ASP and MTTC are in Cho's attacker-side effectiveness list.

claim: ASP is the dominant effectiveness metric.
quote: the attack success probability (e.g., whether an attacker achieved its goal of a launched attack such as ﬁnding a vulnerable target) is a dominant metric used for the effectiveness of MTD ... the payoff or utility of attackers or defenders is also one of the dominant metrics used in the existing MTD techniques
locator: Sec. VII-A, Figs. 6-7, p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21)
issue: Cho says 'a dominant metric' and names utility as 'also one of the dominant metrics'; 'the dominant' overstates. Fig. 6 does make ASP the largest attacker-side slice (12 of 30), but the defender-side 'system security' group (14, Fig. 7) is larger. Scope dropped too: 27 papers, 2011-2018.
fix_text: "ASP is the dominant effectiveness metric" -> "ASP is the most used attacker-side effectiveness metric" (or "a dominant")

claim: Efficiency metrics measure the cost of an attack or of MTD.
quote: although both metrics are concerned about resources the attacker needs to invest to launch a planned attack ... This metric measures how much overhead is introduced to deploy a given MTD
issue: Defender-side also includes QoS to users, which is a cost of MTD in service terms; holds.

claim: No standard set of MTD metrics exists.
quote: However, no standard metrics have been proposed to measure their effectiveness and efﬁciency.
issue: Cho's words carry the claim as of its 2019 submission ('have been proposed'); the present tense 'exists' in 2026 needs a newer source. The next sentence's jalowski2026 may carry it (not checked in this pass).
fix_text: "No standard set of metrics exists \citep{cho2020}" -> "... \citep{cho2020, jalowski2026}" if Jalowski says so; else "No standard set of metrics had been proposed by 2020 \citep{cho2020}"

claim: Table 3.1's 2x2 frame (effectiveness/efficiency x attacker/defender) is Cho's classification.
quote: We discuss the metrics to measure the effectiveness of MTD techniques in terms of the perspectives of an attacker and a defender.

claim: The examples in the table are from the works surveyed, placed as Cho classifies them.
quote: The metrics to measure the effectiveness of existing MTD techniques are summarized in Figs. 6 and 7 based on 27 papers published during 2011-2018.
issue: Right after '[cho2020]', 'the works surveyed' reads as Cho's corpus, but many examples postdate Cho (kim2026, masud2025, zhang2023, ho2024, tay2024) and their cell placement (NCR, risk, mitigation factor, time since last MTD, attack actions blocked, attack path metrics) is ours, applying Cho's frame. 'As Cho et al. classify them' can be read as Cho placing these metrics.
fix_text: "with examples from the works surveyed" -> "with examples from the works this chapter surveys"

claim: ASP is an attacker-side effectiveness metric.
quote: Attack success probability (ASP) [3], [11], [22], [25], [26], [28], [32], [45], [49], [136], [147], [173]: This metric refers to the probability that attacks are successfully performed.
issue: Survey cited for the metric's place in the classification, not for a finding; appropriate.

claim: MTTC is an attacker-side effectiveness metric.
quote: Mean time to compromise a system (MTTC) [4], [26], [27], [32], [186]: This indicates how long an attacker takes to compromise an entire system.
issue: Cho also notes MTTC equals the defender-side MTTF; placement attacker-side matches Cho's list.

claim: Attack utility is an attacker-side effectiveness metric.
quote: Attack utility [5], [6], [22], [119], [134], [181], [182]: When the interactions between attackers and defenders and their best strategies are considered based on game theoretic approaches, the payoff (or utility) of an attacker is used to measure the gain or loss by deploying a proposed MTD.

claim: Defence success probability is a defender-side effectiveness metric.
quote: Defense success probability (DSP) [3], [35], [38], [173]: We call metrics measuring the success of an MTD technique DSP in this work.
issue: DSP is Cho's own umbrella name for heterogeneous success measures.

claim: (uncited) The GA attacker is not an agent: it appears only as the attack resilience the fitness function scores.
quote: Based on the attack resilience, a top ranked computer conﬁguration is selected. ... developing a ﬁtness function that can provide a diverse solution space for design decisions in MTD techniques is not a trivial task
locator: Sec. VI-B, p. 725 printed (PDF p. 17); p. 726 printed (PDF p. 18)
issue: Rests on Cho's report of Crouse and Fulp; 'not an agent' is the dissertation's reading, and it reads as such. Inherits U0194's generalisation from one study to all GAs.

claim: (uncited) The attacker model decides which deployment strategy is optimal.
quote: The differences between optimal strategies can be explained by the attack model each study used and more speciﬁcally whether the attacker’s goal required a persistent foothold in the system.
issue: Cho says this directly (Carter vs Colbaugh and Glass), but the cite sits on the next sentence's Carter example (U0199). Cho's general claim is better support than the example.
fix_text: "which deployment strategy is optimal." -> "which deployment strategy is optimal \citep{cho2020}."

claim: (uncited) Effectiveness metrics measure how well MTD stops the attacker.
quote: The attacker’s metric estimates its attack performance, indicating that the attacker’s high performance refers to the defender’s low performance, and vice-versa.
issue: Covered by the cho2020 citation two sentences earlier (U0202).

claim: (cited to zhang2023 only) Defender-side effectiveness metrics measure the network's security.
quote: The defender’s metric measures its performance in achieving security and defense goals of a given system.
issue: The definition of the defender-side class is Cho's; zhang2023 supports only the NCR example. Not a defect if the paragraph's earlier cho2020 is read as covering it.
